An average is meant to tell you the typical value. So take ten salaries at a small company, from forty-two to sixty-five thousand. Their mean is fifty-three point seven thousand. Their median, the middle value, is fifty-three and a half. Almost the same. Now the CEO walks in, earning a million. The mean leaps to a hundred and thirty-nine point seven thousand. The median just moves to fifty-five. Ten of the eleven people earn less than the mean. It describes almost nobody in the room. That's because the mean is a balance point. Put one heavy value far out, and the balance point slides toward it. The median only asks who's in the middle. It doesn't care how far out the CEO sits. And money nearly always has a tail like that.

Here are five hundred customer orders. Most are modest, with a long tail stretching off to the right. The median order is about twenty-three dollars. The mean is twenty-six fifty-eight. The tail drags it up. So a mean above the median is a free alarm for skew. The wider the gap, the more you should lead with the median. Which center is right? That depends on the data. Symmetric, with no wild values? The mean uses everything, and works well. Skewed, like incomes, prices and wait times? The median is the honest typical value. Categories? Only the most common one, the mode, makes sense. And two peaks? Then no single center will do. But even the right center hides how much the values move.
